video_title: The Race to Build the Private Ethereum
gist: Aztec co-founder Zac Williamson tells Bankless's David Hoffman that Aztec is the only privacy-preserving smart contract chain besides Zcash (which offers private money rather than smart contracts) with no protocol-level backdoors or viewing keys. He argues that privacy will win as a requirement rather than a feature. On his account it enables compliant, composable on-chain RWAs and identity (ZK Passport) instead of today's siloed 'off-chain mega apps', and AI-driven exploits will push activity onto formally verified, trustless infrastructure. He outlines the Aztec Tiara upgrade (proving time halved, 6-12s soft finality) and 2027 goals (5-minute hard finality, real-time proving).

insights.claim: Williamson says there is a race to become 'the private Ethereum', a smart contract chain with strong privacy, analogous to Zcash's position as private digital gold. Many protocols advertise privacy loosely without delivering quality privacy.
insights.speaker: Zac Williamson
insights.so_what: Privacy chains should be compared on the quality of their guarantees, not on marketing claims.
insights.quote: there is a I would say a race to be the private Ethereum

insights.claim: Williamson claims that, outside of Zcash, Aztec is the only privacy-preserving blockchain with no backdoors, centralized actors or third-party viewing keys, and offers to publicly debate anyone who disagrees.
insights.speaker: Zac Williamson
insights.so_what: Aztec is positioning as the leading credibly neutral private smart contract chain.
insights.quote: outside of Zcash, we're the only um privacy preserving blockchain that doesn't have back doors in them

insights.claim: Williamson gives two reasons most private chains use viewing keys or trusted operators. Fully decentralized private transactions are technically hard because of the zero-knowledge proof load, and integration partners such as Circle demand viewing keys plugged into compliance monitoring like TRM.
insights.speaker: Zac Williamson
insights.so_what: Pressure from integration partners pushes most privacy projects toward surveillance-compatible designs.

insights.claim: Williamson says Aztec has no viewing keys at the protocol level, but applications such as banks can build their own viewing keys into their app code, keeping the network neutral while allowing compliance at the application layer.
insights.speaker: Zac Williamson
insights.so_what: Institutions can meet compliance requirements at the app level without compromising the base layer.

insights.claim: Williamson says Aztec launched as a stage two rollup on Ethereum because a privacy network that is not fully decentralized creates centralized actors who are obliged to surveil and censor.
insights.speaker: Zac Williamson
insights.so_what: Full decentralization is a precondition for credible privacy.

insights.claim: Williamson says individuals don't pay for privacy: given two comparable products, users pick the cheaper, better-UX one even if it harvests their data, which he calls a tragedy-of-the-commons situation.
insights.speaker: Zac Williamson
insights.so_what: Pitching privacy as a consumer feature won't drive adoption.

insights.claim: Williamson's thesis is that privacy wins because it enables applications that cannot exist without it, eventually most of traditional finance, such as tokenized mortgages and bonds that require knowing the holder.
insights.speaker: Zac Williamson
insights.so_what: Institutional tokenization of real-world assets is the main adoption driver for private chains.
insights.quote: privacy is going to win because it enables products and applications that cannot exist without it

insights.claim: Williamson argues that the 'institutionalization of crypto' is really crypto moving off-chain into proprietary networks and L2s with data custodians. He says this sacrifices composability and produces vertically integrated 'off-chain mega apps', citing Robinhood Chain, Hyperliquid and Polymarket.
insights.speaker: Zac Williamson
insights.so_what: Siloed liquidity limits crypto's growth, and that value is not captured by decentralized chains like Ethereum.
insights.quote: What's really happening is crypto is moving offchain

insights.claim: Williamson says the fix for compliant composability is to put KYC and credential data on-chain encrypted, so any app can query it without needing a relationship with each data custodian. He acknowledges the standards have to be built nearly from scratch.
insights.speaker: Zac Williamson
insights.so_what: Shared on-chain credentials could reduce the fragmentation of liquidity across apps.
insights.quote: You put the data on chain and you don't worry about it because it's encrypted and it's private

insights.claim: ZK Passport reads a passport's chip and matches the user's face on their phone, then sends only a zero-knowledge proof, for example 'citizen of country X' or 'not on a sanctions list', instead of raw passport data. The proof can be stored as a reusable credential on Aztec for any smart contract to query.
insights.speaker: Zac Williamson
insights.so_what: Enables sanctions screening for tokenized securities without exposing users' data.

insights.claim: Hoffman and Williamson agree that public-chain credentials fail because enough on-chain activity lets observers deduce who is behind a credential, so privacy is needed even when only a credential is posted.
insights.speaker: David Hoffman / Zac Williamson
insights.so_what: Compliance tools on transparent chains have a built-in privacy leak.

insights.claim: Hoffman notes that over 99% of crypto transactions still occur on public ledgers and the expected flip to private chains has not happened. Williamson believes the flip can happen, and Hoffman hopes for 90/10 by end of 2027.
insights.speaker: David Hoffman / Zac Williamson
insights.so_what: Private chains are a large opportunity but adoption so far is minimal.

themes.theme: AI exploits and the trusted-operator model

insights.claim: Williamson argues AI agents can now be spun up in the millions, possibly billions soon, to find and autonomously exploit vulnerabilities that once required highly paid experts. That makes even small, obscure targets, like an old PHP server running a $10,000 order book, worth attacking.
insights.speaker: Zac Williamson
insights.so_what: Relying on obscurity for security is ending, and breach risk rises across the web.
insights.quote: It's worth an AI agent's time to look into that now

insights.claim: Williamson predicts that the internet's trusted-operator model will be destroyed and that trust in websites holding card details or passports will rapidly erode.
insights.speaker: Zac Williamson
insights.so_what: Demand should grow for trustless, minimal-third-party infrastructure.
insights.quote: The whole trusted operator model or the internet is going to get destroyed

insights.claim: Williamson argues blockchains, which already operate in adversarial environments, will harden much faster than the rest of the internet, though they are not immune, as the Binance hack showed. Zcash's circuits and large parts of Aztec's protocol are already formally verified.
insights.speaker: Zac Williamson
insights.so_what: Formal verification is becoming urgent rather than optional.

insights.claim: Williamson says private chains benefit more than public ones from the move away from trusted operators. Migrating web2 systems on-chain requires sensitive and proprietary data, which would draw lawsuits on transparent chains like Ethereum or Solana.
insights.speaker: Zac Williamson
insights.so_what: Privacy lets more web2 activity move on-chain.
insights.quote: you'll get sued by 50 million people because you just put all their sensitive data um on a transparent network

insights.claim: Williamson frames encrypted user-held credentials as risk arbitrage: if only the user holds the decryption keys, the data is not the application's, so the app no longer carries the risk of holding hackable data.
insights.speaker: Zac Williamson
insights.so_what: Apps can offload data liability by building on private chains.

insights.claim: Williamson warns that AI is making it far cheaper to analyze public on-chain transaction, trade and portfolio data adversarially, so minimizing on-chain data exposure improves safety, for example protecting good DeFi traders from copy-trading.
insights.speaker: Zac Williamson
insights.so_what: Private yield and trading products are a near-term draw for retail users.

insights.claim: Aztec launched in April. The Aztec Tiara upgrade halves proving time (over a 100% performance gain), brings soft finality of about 6-12 seconds, and adds more formal verification after months of 24/7 AI code audits.
insights.speaker: Zac Williamson
insights.so_what: Private transactions are approaching Ethereum-like user experience.

insights.claim: Client-side proof generation for a private transaction currently takes about 5 seconds in a web browser and about 1 second in a native app, which is the main latency cost of privacy.
insights.speaker: Zac Williamson
insights.so_what: Proof generation is the main remaining UX bottleneck for private transactions.
insights.quote: that takes roughly 5 seconds in a web browser on my machine. Um takes 1 second if I'm running a native app

insights.claim: For 2027, Aztec aims to cut hard finality and withdrawal time from 40 minutes to 5 minutes, offer instant withdrawals for a tip of about 10-20 cents, reach real-time proving, and fully formally verify the protocol.
insights.speaker: Zac Williamson
insights.so_what: Faster exits would make Aztec more usable for DeFi.

insights.claim: The AZTEC token is used for gas, staking for validators, and governance. A recent governance change fixed overpayment to provers, and Williamson expects the extra cost of privacy for network operators to trend toward zero.
insights.speaker: Zac Williamson
insights.so_what: The token's economics look like a standard proof-of-stake token, with prover costs falling.

insights.claim: Williamson acknowledges MEV can exist on Aztec because trading protocols must be partly public for price discovery. Multi-party computation solutions are being explored but are a later-stage effort.
insights.speaker: Zac Williamson
insights.so_what: Privacy does not yet remove MEV.

insights.claim: Aztec is targeting web3-native users first and plans to court Wall Street only after a few more months of hardening, so that it can offer institutions a turnkey, white-label, fully formally verified product.
insights.speaker: Zac Williamson
insights.so_what: Institutional adoption of Aztec is a 2027-or-later story.

insights.claim: Williamson lists upcoming Aztec products including private yield (zk.money), private AI inference payments, private perps and futures, under-collateralized lending using private identity and reputation, and a fully native private stablecoin with private issuance and settlement.
insights.speaker: Zac Williamson
insights.so_what: Aztec's app ecosystem is expanding into private DeFi primitives.
